title: Der alte Hildebrand
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 95. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in South German (Bavarian-Austrian) dialect; the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form. The glosses in round brackets inside the text — Armon (Eiermann), dacket (einfältig) — are the Grimms’ own and belong to the 1857 text.
about: KHM 95, printed wholly in South German (Bavarian-Austrian) dialect rather than the High German of most of the collection, so the spelling looks unfamiliar from the very first line. A lovesick parson talks a farmer’s wife into a fake illness and a sham pilgrimage sermon so he can have the house to himself, and sends her husband — Hildebrand — off toward the fictitious Göckerliberg with a sack of bay leaves and a kreuzer. An egg-seller gossip smuggles the suspicious husband home hidden in his own egg basket, and the tale ends as a song: parson and wife singing gaily of their stolen evening while Hildebrand, still hidden in the basket, sings back before climbing out to beat the parson out of the house.

sentences.t: Es war amahl a Baur und a Bäurin, und dö Bäurin, dö hat der Pfarra im Dorf gern gesegn, und da hat er alleweil gwunschen, wann er nur amahl an ganzen Tag mit der Bäurin allan recht vergnügt zubringa kunnt, und der Bäurin der wars halt a recht gwesn.
sentences.l: There was once a farmer and a farmer’s wife, and the farmer’s wife — the parson in the village liked to see her, and so he was always wishing that he might just once spend a whole day with the farmer’s wife alone and right merrily, and to the farmer’s wife that would have been quite all right too.
sentences.i: There was once a farmer and his wife, and the parson of the village was fond of the wife, and was forever wishing that he might for once spend a whole day alone with her and merry; and the wife would have had nothing against it either.
sentences.n: This tale is printed from beginning to end in a South German — Bavarian-Austrian — dialect, so that nearly every word looks a little foreign beside the High German of the rest of the collection; the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each form. Here: amahl = einmal, a = ein, Baur = Bauer, dö = die, Pfarra = Pfarrer, alleweil = allweil, always, gwunschen = gewünscht, an = einen, allan = allein, zubringa = zubringen, kunnt = könnte, gwesn = gewesen — and the second a, in “der wars halt a recht gwesn,” is auch, also, not an article. “gern gesegn (gesehen) haben” is to be fond of someone. The noun set out first and then taken up again by a pronoun — “dö Bäurin, dö hat …” — is how this speech builds a sentence, and it happens all through the tale.

sentences.t: No, da hat er amahl zu der Bäurin gsagt „hanz, mei liebi Bäurin, hietzt hab i was ausstudiert, wie wir halt amahl an ganzen Tag recht vergnügt mitanander zubringa kunnten.
sentences.l: Well, then said he once to the farmer’s wife “now then, my dear farmer’s wife, now I have thought out something, how we might for once spend a whole day right merrily with one another.
sentences.i: Well, one day he said to the farmer’s wife: “Now then, my dear wife, I have thought out a way for the two of us to spend a whole day together and merry.
sentences.n: No = nun, well; hietzt = jetzt, now; i = ich, not the interjection ei; ausstudiert is thought out, worked out. hanz is an attention-catching particle of this dialect — now then, look here — and its origin is not settled; it opens three speeches in the tale. mitanander = miteinander, kunnten = könnten.

sentences.t: Wißts was, ös legts eng aufm Mittwoch ins Bett und sagts engern Mon ös seits krang, und lamatierts und übelts nur recht, und das treibts fort bis aufm Sunta, wann i die Predi halt,
sentences.l: You know what, you lay yourself in bed on Wednesday and tell your husband you are ill, and lament and make out to be poorly right thoroughly, and keep that up until Sunday, when I hold the sermon,
sentences.i: I tell you what: on Wednesday you take to your bed and tell your husband you are ill, and moan and carry on properly, and keep it up until Sunday, when I preach the sermon;
sentences.n: Every one of these verbs is a plural imperative with the pronoun swallowed into it: ös = ihr, and legts, sagts, lamatierts, übelts, treibts are legt ihr, sagt ihr, lamentiert ihr, übelt ihr, treibt ihr — this dialect addresses one person as ihr and glues the ending on. eng = euch, engern = eurem, Mon = Mann, seits = seid, krang = krank, aufm = am, Predi = Predigt. übeln is to be poorly, to make out that one is ill.

sentences.t: und da wir (werde) i predigen daß wer z’ Haus a krangs Kind, an krangen Mon, a krangs Weib, an krangen Vader, a krange Muader, a krange Schwester, Bruader, oda wers sunst nacha is, hat, und der thut a Wollfart aufm Göckerliberg in Wälischland, wo ma um an Kreuzer an Metzen Lorberbladen kriegt, dem wirds krange Kind, der krange Mon, ’s krange Weib, der krange Vader, d’ krange Muader, d’ krange Schwester, oda wers sunst nacha is, auf der Stell gsund.“
sentences.l: and then will (werde) I preach that whoever has at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister, brother, or whoever else it may be, and he makes a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where for a kreuzer one gets a peck of bay leaves, for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister, or whoever else it may be, becomes well on the spot.”
sentences.i: and then I shall preach that whoever has at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister or brother, or whoever else it may be, and makes a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where a peck of bay leaves costs a kreuzer — for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister, or whoever else it may be, will be well on the spot.”
sentences.n: The round brackets round (werde) are the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text to gloss the dialect wir for readers outside the south; they do this several times in the tale, and such brackets are never ours. The sermon is a formula and will be said over four times, hardly changed, and that repetition is the joke, so it is kept in full. Welschland is the Romance country over the Alps, Italy; the Göckerliberg is a nowhere mountain, and a Göckerl is a young cock, so the name is roughly Cockerel Hill. Ein Metzen is an old dry measure of grain, a large one — in Austria upwards of fifty litres — and it is rendered here by the homely English peck; Lorberbladen are Lorbeerblätter, bay leaves, and a whole measure of them for a kreuzer, the smallest coin there was, is worth nothing, and the point of the errand is only its distance. “auf der Stell” = auf der Stelle, on the spot.

sentences.t: „Dös wir i schon machen“ hat die Bäurin drauf gsagt.
sentences.l: “That will I do right enough” said the farmer’s wife to that.
sentences.i: “I shall manage that,” said the farmer’s wife.
sentences.n: dös = das; wir is werde, will — the very form the Grimms glossed a line ago; schon in this position is not “already” but the particle of confidence, right enough, never fear.

sentences.t: No, drauf, aufm Mittwoch hat sie halt d’ Bäurin ins Bett glegt und hat glamatiert und gübelt als wie, und ihr Mon hat ihr alles braucht, was er nur gwißt hat, ’s hat aber halt nix gholfn.
sentences.l: Well, thereupon, on the Wednesday the farmer’s wife laid herself in bed and lamented and made out to be poorly as anything, and her husband applied to her everything that he only knew of, but it just did not help at all.
sentences.i: Well, on the Wednesday the wife took to her bed and moaned and made out to be ill as anything, and her husband tried on her every remedy he knew, but nothing was any use.
sentences.n: In “hat sie halt d’ Bäurin ins Bett glegt,” sie stands for sich, the reflexive — she laid herself in bed. “als wie” at the end has nothing following it and works as a plain intensifier, like “as anything.” brauchen here has its older sense of applying or using a remedy, not needing. glegt = gelegt, glamatiert = lamentiert, gübelt = geübelt, gwißt = gewußt, gholfn = geholfen: the ge- of the participle is worn down to a bare g- all through this tale. halt is the southern particle of resignation — just, simply — and it is everywhere.

sentences.t: Wie denn der Sunta kuma is, hat d’ Bäurin gsagt „mir is zwar so miserabel als ob i glei verschaden sollt, aber ans möcht i do no vor mein End, i möcht halt in Herrn Pfarra sei Predi hörn, dö er heund halten wird.“
sentences.l: When then the Sunday came, said the farmer’s wife “I feel so wretched, to be sure, as if I were about to pass away at once, but one thing should I still like before my end, I should like to hear the lord parson’s sermon that he will hold today.”
sentences.i: When Sunday came, the wife said: “I feel so wretched, to be sure, as if I were about to die on the spot; but there is one thing I should still like before my end — I should like to hear the parson’s sermon that he is preaching today.”
sentences.n: verschaden = verscheiden, to pass away. ans here is eins, one thing — not the High German ans, “to the”; this dialect is full of such traps, and each word has to be read for what it means here. do no = doch noch, still. “in Herrn Pfarra sei Predi” is the possessive built with a dative and a following pronoun — dem Herrn Pfarrer seine Predigt — which is how southern German owns a thing; sei is sein, his, not the imperative “be.” heund = heute, hörn = hören.

sentences.t: „A, mei Kind,“ sagt der Baur drauf, „thu du dös nit, du kunntst schlechter wern, wann aufstundst.
sentences.l: “Ah, my child,” says the farmer to that, “do not you do that, you might get worse, if you got up.
sentences.i: “Ah, my dear,” said the farmer, “don’t you do that — you might get worse if you got up.
sentences.n: A = ach, mei = mein, nit = nicht, kunntst = könntest, wern = werden, aufstundst = aufstündest; schlechter here is the comparative, worse, not the plain adjective schlecht. In “wann aufstundst” the du is left out altogether and lives only in the -st of the verb, which this dialect does freely. Husband and wife call each other mei Kind without any thought of age.

sentences.t: Schau, es wir i in d’Predi gehn und wir recht acht gebe und wir dir alles wieder derzöhln, was der Herr Pfarra gsagt hat.“
sentences.l: Look, I will go to the sermon and will pay right good heed and will tell you again everything that the lord parson has said.”
sentences.i: Look, I will go to the sermon, and I will pay good heed and tell you again everything the parson has said.”
sentences.n: Schau is the imperative of schauen, look — not die Schau, a show. wir is again werde, I will, three times over in this one sentence. The little es before it has no work to do in the English and may be no more than a filler of speech; d’Predi is printed here without a space and elsewhere with one. “acht gebe” is Acht geben, to pay attention; derzöhln = erzählen, with the southern der- for er-.

sentences.t: „No,“ hat d’ Bäurin gsagt, „so geh halt und gib recht Acht und derzöhl mir alles, was d’ ghört hast.“
sentences.l: “Well,” said the farmer’s wife, “then just go and pay good heed and tell me everything that you have heard.”
sentences.i: “Well then,” said the wife, “go along, and pay good heed, and tell me everything you have heard.”
sentences.n: d’ here is du, not the article die — the same clipped letter does both jobs in this tale, and only the sentence says which. ghört = gehört.

sentences.t: No, und da is der Baur halt in d’ Predi ganga, und da hat der Herr Pfarra also an gfangt zun predigen und hat halt gsagt, wann ans a krangs Kind, an krangen Mon, a krangs Weib, an krangen Vader, a krange Muader, a krange Schwester, Bruader, oda wers sunst nacha war, z’ Haus hät, und der wollt a Wollfart machen aufm Göckerliberg in Wälischland, wo der Metzen Lorberbladen an Kreuzer kost, dem wirds krange Kind, der krange Mon, ’s krange Weib, der krange Vader, d’ krange Muader, d’ krange Schwester, Bruader, oda wers sunst nacha war, auf der Stell gesund wern,
sentences.l: Well, and so the farmer went to the sermon, and there the lord parson began thus to preach and said that if one had at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister, brother, or whoever else it might be, and he wanted to make a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where the peck of bay leaves costs a kreuzer, for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister, brother, or whoever else it might be, would become well on the spot,
sentences.i: Well, so the farmer went to the sermon, and the parson began to preach, and said that if anyone had at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister or brother, or whoever else it might be, and would make a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where a peck of bay leaves costs a kreuzer, then for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister or brother, or whoever else it might be, would be well on the spot,
sentences.n: The formula comes round for the second of four times, and hardly a word of it moves. ans here is einer, anyone; “an gfangt” is angefangen with the separable an standing apart; zun = zum, zu dem, before an infinitive used as a noun; kost is kostet, costs, not die Kost, food. hät is hätte, and war stands for wäre — the subjunctive of reported speech, since all of this is what the parson said.

sentences.t: und wer also dö Ras unternehma wollt, der soll nach der Meß zu ihm kuma, da wird er ihm den Lorbersack gebn und den Kreuzer.
sentences.l: and whoever then wanted to undertake the journey, he should come to him after the mass, then will he give him the bay-sack and the kreuzer.
sentences.i: and whoever wished to undertake the journey should come to him after mass, and he would give him the bay-leaf sack and the kreuzer.
sentences.n: Ras = Reise, the journey; Meß = Messe, the mass. The parson has provided for everything, sack and coin both, which is the measure of how badly he wants the farmer out of the house.

sentences.t: Da war niembd fröher als der Bauer, und nach der Meß is er gleich zum Pfarra ganga, und der hat ihm also den Lorbersack gebn und den Kreuzer.
sentences.l: Then was nobody gladder than the farmer, and after the mass he went straight to the parson, and he gave him the bay-sack and the kreuzer.
sentences.i: Nobody was gladder than the farmer, and after mass he went straight to the parson, who gave him the bay-leaf sack and the kreuzer.
sentences.n: niembd = niemand. fröher is froher, gladder, from froh — not früher, earlier, which the eye wants to see. Bauer is spelt out in full here and Baur everywhere else; both stand as printed.

sentences.t: Drauf is er nach Haus kuma und hat schon bei der Hausthür eini gschrien „juchesha, liebes Weib, hietzt is so viel als obs gsund warst.
sentences.l: Thereupon he came home and shouted in already at the house door “hurrah, dear wife, now it is as good as if you were well.
sentences.i: Then he came home and shouted in at the front door: “Hurrah, dear wife, now it is as good as if you were well.
sentences.n: eini = herein, in; the little direction-words — eini, eina — carry much of the motion in this speech. juchesha is a shout of joy, juchhe. “so viel als ob” is as good as. In “als obs gsund warst” the reading taken here is “as if you were well”; the clipped obs would also allow “as if it were well,” and the tale does not settle it.

sentences.t: Der Herr Pfarra hat heunt predigt, daß wer a krangs Kind, an krangen Mon, a kranges Weib, an krangen Vader, a krange Muader, a krange Schwester, Bruader, oda wers sunst nacha war, z’ Haus hat, und der macht a Wollfart aufm Göckerliberg in Wälischland, wo der Metzen Lorberbladen an Kreuzer kost, dem wird ’s krange Kind, der krange Mon, ’s krange Weib, der krange Vader, d’ krange Muader, d’ krange Schwester, Bruader, oda wers sunst nacha war, auf der Stell gsund;
sentences.l: The lord parson preached today, that whoever has at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister, brother, or whoever else it might be, and he makes a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where the peck of bay leaves costs a kreuzer, for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister, brother, or whoever else it might be, becomes well on the spot;
sentences.i: The parson preached today that whoever has at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister or brother, or whoever else it may be, and makes a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where a peck of bay leaves costs a kreuzer — for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister or brother, or whoever else it may be, will be well on the spot;
sentences.n: The formula a third time, now in the farmer’s mouth, and he has it by heart. heunt = heute, which the tale spelt heund a few lines above; predigt stands for gepredigt, with the participle’s ge- gone altogether. The apostrophe in “’s krange Kind” is the article das worn down to a single letter.

sentences.t: und hietzt hab i mir schon den Lorbersack gholt vom Herrn Pfarra und den Kreuzer, und wir glei mein Wanderschaft antreten, daß d’ desto ehender gsund wirst;“
sentences.l: and now have I already fetched myself the bay-sack from the lord parson and the kreuzer, and will set out on my journey at once, so that you get well all the sooner;”
sentences.i: and now I have already got the bay-leaf sack from the parson, and the kreuzer, and I will set out on my travels at once, so that you get well all the sooner.”
sentences.n: wir is werde once more. “mir … gholt” is the dative of interest, fetched for myself. antreten is separable and stands split; “eine Wanderschaft antreten” is to set out on a journey. ehender = eher, sooner; d’ here is again du.

sentences.t: und drauf is er fort ganga.
sentences.l: and thereupon he went off.
sentences.n: ganga = gegangen; the participle of gehen keeps no ge- at all in this dialect.

sentences.t: Er war aber kam fort, so is die Bäurin schon auf gwesn, und der Pfarra war a glei do.
sentences.l: He was however hardly gone, when the farmer’s wife was already up, and the parson was there at once too.
sentences.i: But he was hardly gone when the wife was up out of bed, and the parson was there at once as well.
sentences.n: kam = kaum, hardly. “auf gwesn” is to be up, out of bed. a = auch, also, too — not the English article, which the eye keeps wanting; do = da, there.

sentences.t: Hietz lassen wir aber dö zwa indessen auf der Seiten und gänga mir mit’n Baur.
sentences.l: Now let us however leave those two aside meanwhile and go we along with the farmer.
sentences.i: But now let us leave those two aside for the while, and go along with the farmer.
sentences.n: The teller steps out of the tale for a moment to move us from one place to the other. Hietz is hietzt without its t. mir here is wir, we — not the dative mir, to me — and gänga is gehen. mit’n = mit dem, zwa = zwei.

sentences.t: Der is halt alleweil drauf los ganga, damit er desto ehender aufm Göckerliberg kummt, und wie halt so geht, begegnt ihm sein Gvatter.
sentences.l: He just walked straight on all the while, so that he might come to the Göckerliberg all the sooner, and as it just goes, his gossip meets him.
sentences.i: He walked straight on and on, so as to reach the Göckerliberg all the sooner; and as things go, he met his gossip.
sentences.n: drauflosgehen is to walk straight ahead without looking about one. “wie halt so geht” leaves out its es — as things go, as it happens. Der Gevatter is the man bound to another by standing godfather to his child; gossip is the old English word for exactly that, and the two address each other by the name all through the tale.

sentences.t: Sein Gvatter dös war an Armon (Eiermann), und der is just von Mark kuma, wo er seine Ar verkauft hat.
sentences.l: His gossip, that was an Armon (egg-man), and he had just come from the market, where he had sold his eggs.
sentences.i: His gossip was an egg-man, and he had just come from the market, where he had sold his eggs.
sentences.n: The round brackets round (Eiermann) are the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text to explain the dialect Armon; Ar = Eier, eggs. Mark here is der Markt, the market, not das Mark, marrow. an = einen — einen worn down to two letters, and one of the commonest traps in the tale.

sentences.t: „Globt seist,“ sagt sein Gvatter, „wo gehst denn so trabi hin, Gvatter?“
sentences.l: “Praised be you,” says his gossip, “where are you going then so at a trot, gossip?”
sentences.i: “Praised be Jesus Christ,” says his gossip; “where are you off to in such a hurry, gossip?”
sentences.n: This is the old Catholic country greeting: “Gelobt sei Jesus Christus,” praised be Jesus Christ, cut short to Globt seist; and the farmer’s “In Ewigkeit” in the next speech is the second half of it, in eternity, amen. trabi is trabig, at a trot, from traben.

sentences.t: „In Ewigkeit, Gvatter,“ sagt der Baur, „mein Weib is krang worn, und da hab i heund in Herrn Pfarra sein Predi ghört, und da hat er predigt, daß wann aner z’ Haus an krangs Kind, an krangen Mon, a krangs Weib, an krangen Vader, a krange Muader, a krange Schwester, Bruader, oda wers sunst nacha war, hat, und er macht a Wollfart aufm Göckerliberg in Wälischland, wo der Metzen Lorberbladen an Kreuzer kost, dem wird’s krange Kind, der krange Mon, s’ krange Weib, der krange Vader, d’ krange Muader, d’ krange Schwester, Bruader, oda wers sunst nacha war, auf der Stell gsund, und da hab i mir von Herrn Pfarra den Lorbersack und den Kreuzer gholt, und hietzt trit i halt mein Wanderschaft an.“
sentences.l: “In eternity, gossip,” says the farmer, “my wife has fallen sick, and so today I heard the lord parson’s sermon, and he preached that if anyone has at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister, brother, or whoever else it might be, and he makes a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where the peck of bay leaves costs a kreuzer, for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister, brother, or whoever else it might be, becomes well on the spot, and so have I fetched myself from the lord parson the bay-sack and the kreuzer, and now I am setting out on my journey.”
sentences.i: “In eternity, gossip,” says the farmer; “my wife has fallen sick, and today I heard the parson’s sermon, and he preached that if anyone has at home a sick child, a sick husband, a sick wife, a sick father, a sick mother, a sick sister or brother, or whoever else it may be, and makes a pilgrimage to the Göckerliberg in Welschland, where a peck of bay leaves costs a kreuzer, then for him the sick child, the sick husband, the sick wife, the sick father, the sick mother, the sick sister or brother, or whoever else it may be, will be well on the spot — and so I have got the bay-leaf sack and the kreuzer from the parson, and now I am setting out on my travels.”
sentences.n: The formula a fourth and last time, and the farmer gives it as faithfully as if he were in the pulpit himself. worn = geworden, and “krang worn” is fallen ill. “trit … an” is antreten split, I am setting out. The greeting is completed here: In Ewigkeit, in eternity, is the answer to Globt seist.

sentences.t: „Aber hanz, Gvatter,“ hat der Gvatter zum Baur gsagt, „seits denn ar so dacket (einfältig), daß so was glauben könts?
sentences.l: “But now then, gossip,” said the gossip to the farmer, “are you then so utterly dacket (simple), that you can believe such a thing?
sentences.i: “But look here, gossip,” said the gossip to the farmer, “are you really so simple that you can believe such a thing?
sentences.n: The round brackets round (einfältig) are the Grimms’ own, glossing the dialect dacket, simple-minded. Take care with ar here: it is gar, utterly — not the Ar, eggs, of the sentence before, the same three letters doing two quite different jobs within a few lines. seits = seid ihr, könts = könnt ihr.

sentences.t: Wißts was is?
sentences.l: Do you know what it is?
sentences.n: Wißts = wißt ihr, with the pronoun taken into the verb again; the phrase is the everyday “do you know what?” before a secret is let out.

sentences.t: der Pfarra möcht gern mit engern Weib an ganzen Tag allan recht vergnügt zubringa, drum habn’s eng den Bärn anbunden, daß ihr’en aus’n Füßen kumts.“
sentences.l: the parson would like to spend a whole day alone and right merrily with your wife, and that is why they have tied the bear on you, so that you come out from under his feet.”
sentences.i: the parson would like to spend a whole day alone and merry with your wife, and that is why they have hung this bear on you, to get you out from under his feet.”
sentences.n: “jemandem einen Bären aufbinden,” here anbinden, is to fasten a bear on somebody — the German for spinning a person a tall tale. There is no English idiom to match it, so the bear is left standing in the literal line. habn’s = haben sie, ihr’en = ihr ihm, aus’n = aus den, drum = darum.

sentences.t: „Mein,“ hat der Baur gsagt, „so möcht i do wissen, ob das wahr is.“
sentences.l: “My word,” said the farmer, “then should I like to know whether that is true.”
sentences.i: “Well I never,” said the farmer, “then I should like to know whether that is true.”
sentences.n: Mein! standing alone is not “my” but the southern exclamation — my word, dear me. do = doch.

sentences.t: „No,“ hat der Gvatter gsagt, „wast was, setz di in mein Arkorb eini, so will i di nach Haus tragn, und da wirst es selber segn.“
sentences.l: “Well,” said the gossip, “do you know what, set yourself into my egg-basket, then will I carry you home, and there you will see it yourself.”
sentences.i: “Well,” said the gossip, “I tell you what: get into my egg basket, and I will carry you home, and then you will see it for yourself.”
sentences.n: wast is weißt, you know — not wart, you were. di is dich, yourself, here and again in “will i di … tragn.” Der Arkorb is the Eierkorb, the egg-basket, a deep pannier carried on the back — the Buckelkorb of a few lines further on. eini = hinein, in.

sentences.t: No, das is also gschegn, und den Baur hat sein Gvatter in sein Arkorb eini gsetzt, und der hat’n nach Haus tragn.
sentences.l: Well, so that happened, and the farmer his gossip set into his egg-basket, and he carried him home.
sentences.i: Well, so it was done: the gossip put the farmer into his egg basket and carried him home.
sentences.n: gschegn = geschehen. The object den Baur stands first, ahead of the subject — German may put whatever it likes in front of the verb, and the case endings keep it straight. hat’n = hat ihn; tragn = getragen.

sentences.t: Wie’s nach Haus kuma san, holla, da is schon lusti zuganga.
sentences.l: When they came home, hullo, there it was going merrily already.
sentences.i: When they got home — hullo! — things were merry there already.
sentences.n: Wie’s = wie sie. “es geht lustig zu” is things go merrily, there is a merry time of it; zugehen is impersonal in this use, and zuganga is its participle. holla is a shout of surprise thrown into the sentence.

sentences.t: Da hat die Bäurin schon fast alles, was nur in ihren Hof war, abgstochen ghabt, und Krapfen hats bachen, und der Pfarra war a schon da und hat a sein Geige mitbracht ghabt.
sentences.l: The farmer’s wife had already slaughtered nearly everything that there was at all in her yard, and doughnuts she had baked, and the parson was there already too and had brought his fiddle with him too.
sentences.i: The wife had already killed nearly every creature in the yard, and had baked doughnuts, and the parson was there already, and had brought his fiddle with him.
sentences.n: abstechen is to kill a beast by sticking it — the plain farmyard word, and the tale does not soften it. “abgstochen ghabt” and “mitbracht ghabt” are the double perfect of southern speech, standing for hatte abgestochen, hatte mitgebracht. hats here is hat sie, she, not hat es. Krapfen are the doughnuts fried in fat for a south German feast. a = auch twice over in this sentence.

sentences.t: Und da hat halt der Gvatter anklopft, und d’Bäurin hat gfragt, wer draussen war.
sentences.l: And then the gossip knocked, and the farmer’s wife asked who was outside.
sentences.i: And then the gossip knocked, and the wife asked who was outside.
sentences.n: anklopft = angeklopft, gfragt = gefragt; draussen is draußen, printed with ss here.

sentences.t: „I bins, Gevatterin,“ hat der Gvatter gesagt, „mei, gebts mir heund Nacht a Herberg, i hab meini Ar aufm Mark nit verkauft, und hietzt muß i’s wieder nach Haus trage, und sö san gar z’ schwar, i bring’s nit fort, es is a schon finster.“
sentences.l: “It is I, Mistress Godmother,” said the gossip, “dear me, give me a lodging for this night, I did not sell my eggs at the market, and now must I carry them home again, and they are far too heavy, I cannot get them along, and it is dark already too.”
sentences.i: “It is I, Mistress Godmother,” said the gossip. “Do give me a lodging for tonight; I did not sell my eggs at the market, and now I must carry them home again, and they are far too heavy — I cannot get them along, and it is dark already.”
sentences.n: Die Gevatterin is the woman who stands godmother — the feminine of the Gvatter the two men call each other all through the tale — and the address is Mistress Godmother. heund Nacht is heute Nacht, tonight. Ar and Mark are the eggs and the market again; sö = sie, san = sind, schwar = schwer, z’ = zu, and “i bring’s” is ich bring sie. The basket is heavy for a reason he does not give.

sentences.t: „Ja, mein Gvatter,“ sagt d’ Bäurin drauf, „ös kumts mir recht zur unglegna Zeit.
sentences.l: “Yes, my gossip,” says the farmer’s wife to that, “you come to me at a right inconvenient time.
sentences.i: “Well, gossip,” said the wife, “you come at a most inconvenient time.
sentences.n: kumts = kommt ihr; unglegna is ungelegene, inconvenient, from ungelegen. recht before an adjective is “right, quite,” as in the “recht vergnügt” of the parson’s plan.

sentences.t: No, weils halt her nit anders is, so kömts eina und setzt’s eng dort auf d’ Ofenbank.“
sentences.l: Well, since it just is not otherwise, then come in and set yourselves down there on the stove-bench.”
sentences.i: Well, since it cannot be helped, come in and sit down there on the stove bench.”
sentences.n: weils = weil es. The little her in “weils halt her nit anders is” has no settled reading; the sense of the whole is “since it just is not otherwise,” since there is no help for it. kömts = kommt ihr, eina = herein, “setzt’s eng” = setzt euch. Die Ofenbank is the bench built against the tiled stove, the warm seat of the room and the one furthest from the table.

sentences.t: No hat sie der Gvatter also mit sein Buckelkorb auf d’ Ofenbank gsetzt.
sentences.l: So sat the gossip himself down with his back-basket on the stove-bench.
sentences.i: So the gossip sat down on the stove bench with his back-basket.
sentences.n: sie here is again sich, himself. Der Buckelkorb is the basket carried on the back — der Buckel is the back — and it is the Arkorb of a moment ago, with the farmer still inside it.

sentences.t: Der Pfarra aber und d’ Bäurin dö warn halt recht lusti.
sentences.l: The parson however and the farmer’s wife, those were right merry.
sentences.i: But the parson and the wife were merry enough.
sentences.n: warn = waren, lusti = lustig. The noun set out first and then taken up again by dö is the same doubling as in the tale’s opening sentence.

sentences.t: Endli fangt der Pfarra an und sagt „hanz, mein liebi Bäurin, ös könnts ja so schön singa, singts mir do ans.“
sentences.l: At last begins the parson and says “now then, my dear farmer’s wife, you can sing so beautifully, sing me one.”
sentences.i: At last the parson begins and says: “Now then, my dear woman, you sing so beautifully — sing me one.”
sentences.n: “fangt … an” is anfangen, he begins — the third person present, not an imperative. ans here is eins, one, meaning one song. Endli = endlich, singa = singen, singts = singt ihr.

sentences.t: „A,“ sagt die Bäurin, „hietzt kann i nix mehr singa, ja in mein junge Jahren, da hab i’s wohl könna, aber hietzt is schon vorbei.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” says the farmer’s wife, “now can I sing no more, indeed in my young years I could do it well enough, but now it is over already.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” says the wife, “I can sing no more now; in my young years I could do it well enough, but that is over.”
sentences.n: A here is ach, ah — not the article. könna = gekonnt, been able. She is supposed to be at death’s door, and only coyness is keeping her from the song.

sentences.t: „Ei,“ sagt wieder der Pfarra, „singts do nur a bißl.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” says the parson again, “do just sing a little.”
sentences.i: “Oh come,” says the parson, “just sing a little.”
sentences.n: The Ei that opens the speech is the soft interjection — ah, come now — a different word from the A of the line before, which is ach. “a bißl” = ein bißchen, a little; here a is the article ein, where four lines back it was ach and elsewhere auch — three different words hiding in the same single letter.

sentences.t: No, da fangt die Bäurin an und singt
sentences.l: Well, then begins the farmer’s wife and sings
sentences.i: Well, then the farmer’s wife begins, and sings:
sentences.n: The sentence runs straight into the verse that follows, with no colon and no full stop: the song is the end of the sentence.

sentences.t:
„I hab mein Mon wohl ausgesandt
aufm Göckerliberg in Wälischland.“
sentences.l:
“I have sent my husband well away
to the Göckerliberg in Welschland.”
sentences.i:
“I have packed my husband off and away
to the Göckerliberg in Welschland.”
sentences.n: The four songs of this tale are sung to each other across the room, each of them a couplet, and the last three carry a Halleluja at the end as though they were still in church. wohl here is the particle — well and truly, fairly. ausgesandt is sent out, sent off. aufm is auf den, to the. The German rhyme, ausgesandt with Wälischland, is not carried over: these English lines are here to show what is sung, not to be sung.

sentences.t: Drauf singt der Pfarra
sentences.l: Thereupon sings the parson
sentences.i: Thereupon the parson sings:
sentences.n: drauf = darauf, thereupon — the plain word that carries this tale from one thing to the next.

sentences.t:
„I wollt er blieb da a ganzes Jahr,
was fragt i nach dem Lorbersack.
Halleluja!“
sentences.l:
“I wish he stayed there a whole year,
what do I care for the bay-leaf sack.
Hallelujah!”
sentences.n: “I wollt er blieb” is the plain subjunctive of wollen with a bare clause after it: I wish he would stay. “was frag ich nach” is what do I care for, an old turn still alive in German. The Halleluja belongs in church and is dragged into a very unchurchly song, which is the point of it. These two lines do not rhyme in the German either — Jahr and Lorbersack do not — so nothing is lost in the English.

sentences.t: Hietzt fangt der Gvatter hinten an und singt (da muß i aber derzöhln daß der Baur Hildebrand ghassen hat), singt also der Gvatter
sentences.l: Now begins the gossip at the back and sings (here must I tell, though, that the farmer was called Hildebrand), so the gossip sings
sentences.i: Now the gossip at the back begins to sing — here I must mention that the farmer was called Hildebrand — and so the gossip sings:
sentences.n: The round brackets are the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text: the teller breaks off to supply the farmer’s name, which the next song needs and which the tale has withheld until now, though it stands in the title. ghassen = geheißen, was called. hinten is at the back of the room, on the stove bench. The aside is spoken in the same voice as the rest of the tale, i for ich and all.

sentences.t:
„Ei du, mein lieber Hildebrand,
was machst du auf der Ofenbank?
Halleluja!“
sentences.l:
“Ah, you, my dear Hildebrand,
what are you doing on the stove-bench?
Hallelujah!”
sentences.i:
“Ah, you there, my dear Hildebrand,
what are you doing on the stove bench?
Hallelujah!”
sentences.n: The gossip sings the farmer’s own name across the room, and the two in front hear nothing in it that the man in the basket hears. The question is put as though Hildebrand were sitting on the bench in plain sight — which, in a manner of speaking, he is.

sentences.t: Und hietzt singt der Baur in Korb drinna
sentences.l: And now sings the farmer in the basket, inside
sentences.i: And now the farmer sings from inside the basket:
sentences.n: “in Korb” is in dem Korb, with the article worn down to a single letter, and drinna, drinnen, inside, is added after it for good measure.

sentences.t:
„Hietzt kann i das Singa nimmermehr leiden,
hietzt muß i aus mein Buckelkorb steigen.“
sentences.l:
“Now can I bear this singing no more,
now must I climb out of my back-basket.”
sentences.i:
“Now I can stand this singing no longer;
now I must climb out of my back-basket.”
sentences.n: “etwas nicht leiden können” is to be unable to bear a thing. “das Singa” is the infinitive used as a noun, the singing. This couplet does rhyme in the German, leiden with steigen, and the English keeps the sense and lets the rhyme go.

sentences.t: Und steigt aus’n Korb und prügelt den Pfaffen beim Haus hinaus.
sentences.l: And he climbs out of the basket and thrashes the parson out through the house.
sentences.i: And he climbs out of the basket and beats the parson out of the house.
sentences.n: steigt is the third person, he climbs, with the subject left out once more. Der Pfaffe is the disrespectful word for a priest, and the tale saves it for its last line. “beim Haus hinaus” is out through the house; prügeln with a direction is to drive somebody that way with blows. It ends there, and nothing is said of the wife.

glossary.a: a — ein, a; also auch, too, and ach, ah (Bav.: three words in one letter, never the letter A)
glossary.an: an — einen, a, one (acc. masc.; Bav. an = einen); also the separable prefix an- (an gfangt = angefangen)
glossary.ans: ans — eins / einer, one thing, anyone (Bav.; not an das)
glossary.beim: beim — bei dem, at the; beim Haus hinaus = zum Haus hinaus, out through the house (southern)
glossary.braucht: braucht — gebraucht (brauchen), applied, used (past part. without ge-; older sense, to apply a remedy)
glossary.bring: bring — bringe (fortbringen), (I) carry off (1st sg.; i bring’s nit fort = ich bringe sie nicht fort)
glossary.d: d’ — die / der, the (article clipped to one letter); also du, you
glossary.denn: denn — denn, (particle) then, after all (in questions and after wie; not causal here)
glossary.di: di — dich, you (acc. of du; Bav.)
glossary.do: do — doch, (particle) still, do, surely; also da, there (Bav., not Low German)
glossary.en: ’en — ihm / ihn, him (clitic; ihr’en = ihr ihm)
glossary.eng: eng — euch, you (dat./acc. pl.; Bav. eng = euch, not eng ‘narrow’)
glossary.es: es — es, it (impersonal subject; in ‘es wir i … gehn’ a bare filler)
glossary.fangt: fangt — fängt … an (anfangen), begins (3rd sg. present, unumlauted)
glossary.fragt: fragt — frage (fragen), (I) ask, care (1st sg.; was fragt i nach = was frage ich nach)
glossary.gar: gar — gar, far, quite (intensifier; gar z’ schwar = gar zu schwer, far too heavy)
glossary.gebe: gebe — geben, to give (infinitive after werde; acht gebe = Acht geben, to pay heed)
glossary.hab: hab — habe (haben), (I) have (1st sg. present; hab i = habe ich)
glossary.halt: halt — halt, just, simply (southern particle, everywhere here); in ‘die Predi halt’ it is halte (halten), preach
glossary.hats: hats — hat sie (haben), she has (’s = sie, not es)
glossary.her: her — her, an unexplained particle in ‘weils halt her nit anders is’ (since it just is not otherwise); not directional here
glossary.i: i — ich, I (Bav.; not the interjection ei)
glossary.ihm: ihm — ihm, to him (dative of er; masculine throughout this tale)
glossary.in: in — in, into; also den / dem, the (Bav. article: in Herrn Pfarra sei Predi = dem Herrn Pfarrer seine Predigt)
glossary.ja: ja — ja, yes (in „Ja, mein Gvatter“); elsewhere the particle, surely, after all
glossary.kam: kam — kaum, hardly, scarcely (Bav.; not kam, came)
glossary.kost: kost — kostet (kosten), costs (3rd sg.; not die Kost, fare)
glossary.legts: legts — legt ihr (legen), lay! (pl. imperative with the pronoun glued on; legts eng = legt euch)
glossary.los: los — los (drauflosgehen), straight on (drauf los ganga, walked straight ahead)
glossary.macht: macht — macht (machen), makes, does (3rd sg.; a Wollfart macht = macht eine Wallfahrt)
glossary.mark: mark — der Markt, market (Bav. Mark = Markt; not das Mark, marrow)
glossary.mein: mein — mein, my; standing alone „Mein,“ the southern exclamation, my word, dear me
glossary.mir: mir — mir, to me; in ‘gänga mir’ it is wir, we (Bav.)
glossary.n: ’n — dem / den, the (mit’n = mit dem, aus’n = aus den); also ihn, him (hat’n = hat ihn)
glossary.s: ’s — es or das; also sie, she/they (habn’s = haben sie) and ihr (setzt’s = setzt ihr)
glossary.sagts: sagts — sagt ihr (sagen), tell! (pl. imperative with the pronoun glued on)
glossary.schau: schau — schau! (schauen), look! (imperative sg.; not die Schau, a show)
glossary.schlechter: schlechter — schlechter (schlecht), worse (comparative; schlechter wern = schlechter werden)
glossary.sei: sei — sein, his (possessive; Bav. sei = sein, not the imperative ‘be!’)
glossary.seiten: seiten — die Seite, side (dat. sg. with old -n; auf der Seiten = auf der Seite, aside)
glossary.seits: seits — seid ihr (sein), you are (Bav., pronoun glued on; not ‘says’)
glossary.sie: sie — sich, herself, himself (reflexive here, not ‘she, they’)
glossary.sollt: sollt — sollte (sollen), should, were to (1st sg. subjunctive; als ob i … sollt)
glossary.steigt: steigt — steigt (steigen), climbs out (3rd sg., subject left out)
glossary.stell: stell — die Stelle, spot (auf der Stell = auf der Stelle, on the spot; not the imperative of stellen)
glossary.trage: trage — tragen, to carry (infinitive after muß)
glossary.um: um — um, for (of price: um an Kreuzer = für einen Kreuzer)
glossary.verkauft: verkauft — verkauft (verkaufen), sold (past participle: hat … verkauft)
glossary.war: war — war (sein), was; in the parson’s reported sermon it is wäre, were (subjunctive)
glossary.wars: wars — wär’s = wäre es, it would have been (subjunctive, with gwesn)
glossary.warst: warst — wärst (sein), you were (subjunctive, not the preterite)
glossary.wast: wast — weißt (wissen), you know (2nd sg.; wast was = weißt du was)
glossary.werde: werde — werde (werden), (I) will, shall (1st sg.; the Grimms’ own bracket gloss of the dialect wir)
glossary.wir: wir — werde (werden), (I) will, shall (Bav. wir = werde, glossed by the Grimms); also wir, we
glossary.wollt: wollt — wollte (wollen), wanted, would (3rd sg. and 1st sg. subjunctive here)
